notes.front: What is the alternative minimum tax (AMT)?
notes.back: A separate tax, figured on Form 6251, imposed in addition to the regular tax.
notes.explanation: It applies to taxpayers with certain income that gets favourable treatment, or who qualify for certain deductions.
notes.example: Like a second, stricter calculation of the same year’s tax that is added on when it comes out higher.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 6251 to figure the amount, if any, of your alternative minimum tax (AMT). The AMT is a separate tax that is imposed in addition to your regular tax.

notes.front: When do you have a household employee?
notes.back: When you hire someone to do household work and that worker is your employee: you control what work is done and how.
notes.explanation: Full-time or part-time makes no difference once the worker is your employee.
notes.example: Like a nanny who follows the family’s schedule and instructions, as opposed to a cleaning firm that sets its own methods.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “Do You Have a Household Employee?”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You have a household employee if you hired someone to do household work and that worker is your employee. The worker is your employee if you can control not only what work is done, but how it is done.

notes.front: What is estimated tax?
notes.back: The method used to pay tax on income that isn’t subject to withholding.
notes.explanation: Pub. 505 names self-employment, interest, dividends, rent, gains, prizes and awards as such income.
notes.example: Like paying your own tax in instalments during the year because no employer takes it from your pay.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Estimated Tax for 2025”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: Estimated tax is the method used to pay tax on income that isn't subject to withholding.

notes.front: In estimated tax, what is a safe harbor?
notes.back: A payment level, such as a set share of last year’s tax, that is enough to meet the estimated tax rules.
notes.explanation: Pub. 17 uses the term for the higher-income rule based on prior-year AGI over $150,000.
notes.example: Like a guaranteed pass mark: hit it and no penalty applies, whatever your final bill.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Estimated tax safe harbor for higher income taxpayers”, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: Estimated tax safe harbor for higher income taxpayers. If your 2025 adjusted gross income was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if you are married filing a separate return), you

notes.front: What is income in respect of a decedent (IRD)?
notes.back: Income the decedent would have received had death not occurred that wasn’t properly includible on the final return.
notes.explanation: It is taxed to whoever receives it, not on the decedent’s final return.
introduces: income in respect of a decedent
notes.example: Like a final commission cheque that arrives after the salesperson has died.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Income in Respect of a Decedent”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: All income the decedent would have received had death not occurred that wasn't properly includible on the final return, discussed earlier, is income in respect of a decedent.
uses: income in respect of a decedent

notes.front: What is the net investment income tax (NIIT)?
notes.back: A 3.8% tax on the smaller of net investment income or modified AGI above a threshold, figured on Form 8960.
notes.explanation: The threshold depends on filing status.
notes.example: Like a surcharge on investment income that only higher-income households pay.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025), Net Investment Income Tax, “Overview”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: MAGI that's over an applicable threshold amount, and (b) NII, must pay 3.8% of the smaller of (a) or (b) as their NIIT.

notes.front: What is the Additional Medicare Tax?
notes.back: A 0.9% tax on Medicare wages, railroad retirement compensation and self-employment income above a threshold, figured on Form 8959.
notes.explanation: Wages and self-employment income are combined to test the threshold.
notes.example: Like the ordinary Medicare tax, but an extra slice charged only on pay above a set level.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8959 (2025), Additional Medicare Tax, “Additional Medicare Tax”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: A 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to your Medicare wages, Railroad Retirement Tax Act (RRTA) compensation, and self-employment income above a threshold amount.

notes.front: For a minister, what is a housing allowance?
notes.back: Part of a minister’s pay that the employing church officially designates, in advance, as a rental or housing allowance.
notes.explanation: Ordained, commissioned or licensed ministers may be able to exclude it from income tax.
notes.example: Like a rent allowance in a pay package, but tax-free only if the church names it before paying.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Exclusion of Rental Allowance and Fair Rental Value of a Parsonage”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: ministers of the gospel may be able to exclude from income tax the rental allowance or fair rental value of a parsonage that is provided to them as pay for their services.

notes.front: For 2025, the AMT exemption for a single filer is {{c1::$88,100}}.
notes.explanation: The exemption increased for 2025; joint filers get a larger one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “What’s New: Exemption amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The exemption amount on Form 6251, line 5, has increased to $88,100 ($137,000 if married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $68,500 if married filing separately).

notes.front: For 2025, the AMT exemption for married filing jointly or a qualifying surviving spouse is {{c1::$137,000}}.
notes.explanation: Married filing separately gets half: $68,500.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “What’s New: Exemption amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: has increased to $88,100 ($137,000 if married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $68,500 if married filing separately).

notes.front: Which 2025 AMT exemption applies to a taxpayer who is married filing separately?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the single amount. C is the joint amount.
notes.explanation: Married filing separately has its own figure, half the joint $137,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “What’s New: Exemption amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: ($137,000 if married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $68,500 if married filing separately).

notes.front: Dora’s spouse died in 2023 and she files as a qualifying surviving spouse for 2025. Which AMT exemption applies?
notes.choicesExplained: A is for single filers. B is for married filing separately.
notes.explanation: A qualifying surviving spouse uses the joint amount.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “What’s New: Exemption amount”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: ($137,000 if married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $68,500 if married filing separately).

notes.front: Which form figures the credit for prior year minimum tax?
notes.back: Form 8801.
notes.explanation: Form 6251 figures the AMT itself; Form 8801 figures the later credit.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “Who Must File”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: or the credit for prior year minimum tax (Form 8801).

notes.front: Kenji paid AMT for 2024 and wants to know whether any of it can reduce his 2025 tax. Which form should his preparer look at?
notes.back: B: Form 8801, credit for prior year minimum tax.
notes.choices:
A) Form 6251 only
B) Form 8801
C) Form 8959
notes.choicesExplained: A figures the current year’s AMT. C is the Additional Medicare Tax form.
notes.explanation: Form 6251 works out a single year’s AMT; relief for AMT already paid in an earlier year has its own form.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025), Alternative Minimum Tax—Individuals, “Who Must File”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: or the credit for prior year minimum tax (Form 8801).

notes.front: In 2025, social security and Medicare taxes apply to a household worker you pay {{c1::$2,800}} or more in cash wages.
notes.explanation: Below that amount of cash wages, these taxes don’t apply to that worker.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “What’s New”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Social security and Medicare taxes apply to the wages of household workers you pay $2,800 or more in cash wages in 2025.

notes.front: In 2025 the Patels paid their babysitter, an employee, $2,500 in cash wages; the Kims paid theirs $3,000. Who owes social security and Medicare taxes?
notes.back: B: only the Kims.
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) Only the Kims
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: A: $2,500 is below the threshold. C: $3,000 is over it.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “What’s New”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Social security and Medicare taxes apply to the wages of household workers you pay $2,800 or more in cash wages in 2025.

notes.front: When does a household employer pay federal unemployment tax?
notes.back: When total cash wages to household employees are $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025.
notes.explanation: The tax is on cash wages up to $7,000 a year per employee.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “Table 1. Do You Need To Pay Employment Taxes?”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Pay total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025 to household employees.

notes.front: Must a household employer withhold federal income tax from a household employee’s wages?
notes.back: No: only if the employee asks and the employer agrees.
notes.explanation: This rule was unchanged for 2025.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “What’s New: 2025 federal income tax withholding”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: you're not required to withhold federal income tax from wages you pay a household employee. You should withhold federal income tax only if your household employee asks you to withhold it and you agree.

notes.front: Which worker is most likely your household employee?
notes.back: A: the gardener you control.
notes.choices:
A) A gardener you direct on what to plant and how, on your schedule
B) A lawn company that sends its own crew and methods
notes.choicesExplained: B: you don’t control how the company’s crew does the work.
notes.explanation: The test is control over both what work is done and how.
notes.source: Publication 926 (2025), Household Employer's Tax Guide, “Do You Have a Household Employee?”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The worker is your employee if you can control not only what work is done, but how it is done.

notes.front: In Pub. 505’s flowchart, what first question decides whether you may need to pay 2025 estimated tax?
notes.back: Will you owe $1,000 or more after subtracting withholding and refundable credits from your total tax?
notes.explanation: If not, you are not required to pay estimated tax.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Figure 2-A. Do You Have To Pay Estimated Tax?”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Will you owe $1,000 or more for 2025 after subtracting income tax withholding and refundable credits from your total tax?

notes.front: Under the general rule, withholding and credits of at least {{c1::90%}} of the tax to be shown on the current year’s return avoid the need for estimated tax.
notes.explanation: It is one of two tests; the smaller required amount applies.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Who Must Pay Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: You expect your withholding and tax credits to be less than the smaller of: a. 90% of the tax to be shown on your 2025 tax return, or b. 100% of the tax shown on your 2024 tax return.

notes.front: Under the general rule, the prior-year test is {{c1::100%}} of the tax shown on the prior year’s return, which must cover all 12 months.
notes.explanation: Higher-income taxpayers replace this percentage with 110%.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Who Must Pay Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: b. 100% of the tax shown on your 2024 tax return. Your 2024 tax return must cover all 12 months.

notes.front: When must a taxpayer use 110% instead of 100% of the prior year’s tax?
notes.back: When prior-year AGI was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately).
notes.explanation: The rule doesn’t apply to taxpayers with two-thirds of gross income from farming or fishing.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Higher income taxpayers”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: If your AGI for 2024 was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if your filing status for 2025 is married filing separately), substitute 110% for 100%

notes.front: Mel’s 2024 tax was $10,000 (AGI $90,000). She expects 2025 tax of $14,000 and has $10,500 withheld. Does she meet the safe harbor?
notes.back: A: yes; $10,500 covers 100% of her 2024 tax.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, 100% of prior-year tax
B) No, she needs $12,600
C) No, she needs $14,000
notes.choicesExplained: B (90% of 2025 tax) is only the larger of the two tests; the smaller applies. C is not a test.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Who Must Pay Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: You expect your withholding and tax credits to be less than the smaller of: a. 90% of the tax to be shown on your 2025 tax return, or b. 100% of the tax shown on your 2024 tax return.

notes.front: Paul’s 2024 AGI was $180,000 and his 2024 tax $20,000. He expects 2025 tax of $30,000 and has $21,000 withheld. Is he protected by the prior-year test?
notes.back: B: no; he needs 110% of $20,000, which is $22,000.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, $21,000 exceeds $20,000
B) No, he needs $22,000
notes.choicesExplained: A uses 100%, but his prior-year AGI was over $150,000.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Higher income taxpayers”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: If your AGI for 2024 was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if your filing status for 2025 is married filing separately), substitute 110% for 100%

notes.front: Nia’s 2024 tax was $9,000; she expects 2025 tax of $8,000 and has $7,400 withheld. Does she meet the general rule?
notes.back: A: yes; $7,400 is at least 90% of her 2025 tax.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No
notes.choicesExplained: B: she only needs the smaller of $7,200 and $9,000.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Who Must Pay Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: You expect your withholding and tax credits to be less than the smaller of: a. 90% of the tax to be shown on your 2025 tax return, or b. 100% of the tax shown on your 2024 tax return.

notes.front: What is Form 2210 for, and must most people file it?
notes.back: It figures any penalty for underpaying estimated tax; usually the IRS figures the penalty and you should not file it.
notes.explanation: You may still file it to show the penalty on your return, or must file it in some cases.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2210 (2025), Underpayment of Estimated Tax by Individuals, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 2210 to see if you owe a penalty for underpaying your estimated tax. The IRS will generally figure your penalty for you and you should not file Form 2210.

notes.front: A client may owe an underpayment penalty but wants the IRS to work it out. What should the preparer do?
notes.back: B: leave the line blank and don’t file Form 2210; a bill will follow.
notes.choices:
A) File Form 2210 with the penalty left blank
B) Leave the penalty line blank and not file Form 2210
C) Estimate the penalty and add 10%
notes.choicesExplained: A: Form 2210 isn’t filed when the IRS figures the penalty. C is not a method in the instructions.
notes.explanation: The instructions tell a taxpayer who wants the IRS to figure it to complete the return as usual.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2210 (2025), Underpayment of Estimated Tax by Individuals, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: If you want us to figure the penalty for you, complete your return as usual. Leave the penalty line on your return blank; don't file Form 2210.

notes.front: To request a waiver of the estimated tax penalty, must you file Form 2210?
notes.back: Yes: requesting a waiver is one situation in which you must file it.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the IRS generally figures the penalty itself.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2210 (2025), Underpayment of Estimated Tax by Individuals, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: There are some situations in which you must file Form 2210, such as to request a waiver.

notes.front: For 2025, the maximum self-employment income subject to social security tax is {{c1::$176,100}}.
notes.explanation: Medicare tax has no such cap.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “What’s New”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax is $176,100.

notes.front: Joy has $190,000 of 2025 net earnings from self-employment and no wages. On how much does she pay the social security part of self-employment tax?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the cap. C is the excess above the cap, which is free of social security tax.
notes.explanation: Social security part is capped at $176,100; $190,000 − $176,100 = $13,900 above it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025), “What’s New”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax is $176,100.

notes.front: When can you have excess social security tax withholding for 2025?
notes.back: Only if wages from two or more employers total more than $176,100.
notes.explanation: The test looks at combined wages from two or more employers.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Credit for excess social security”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: you will have excess social security or tier 1 railroad retirement tax withholding for 2025 only if your wages and compensation from two or more employers are more than $176,100.

notes.front: In 2025 Arun earned $100,000 from one employer and $90,000 from another; each withheld social security tax in full. What follows?
notes.back: B: excess withholding, because his combined wages from two employers exceed $176,100.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: withholding was correct
B) He has excess social security withholding
notes.choicesExplained: A: each employer was right alone, but together they withheld on more than the wage base.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Credit for excess social security”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: only if your wages and compensation from two or more employers are more than $176,100.

notes.front: What are the Additional Medicare Tax thresholds?
notes.back: Married filing jointly $250,000; married filing separately $125,000; single, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse $200,000.
notes.explanation: They aren’t indexed for inflation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8959 (2025), Additional Medicare Tax, “Threshold Amounts”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Married filing jointly $250,000 Married filing separately $125,000 Single $200,000 Head of household $200,000

notes.front: On what wages must an employer withhold the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax?
notes.back: On Medicare wages it pays you in excess of $200,000.
notes.explanation: The employer uses $200,000 whatever your filing status.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Credit for excess social security”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: Your employer is responsible for withholding the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on Medicare wages or RRTA compensation it pays to you in excess of $200,000.

notes.front: Grace is single with $230,000 of 2025 wages from one job. What is her Additional Medicare Tax?
notes.choicesExplained: A applies 0.9% to all wages. C ignores that she is over the threshold.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8959 (2025), Additional Medicare Tax, “Additional Medicare Tax”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: A 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to your Medicare wages, Railroad Retirement Tax Act (RRTA) compensation, and self-employment income above a threshold amount.

notes.front: A couple filing jointly each earned $150,000 of wages in 2025. Neither employer withheld Additional Medicare Tax. What do they owe?
notes.choices:
A) $0, as neither is over $200,000
B) $450
C) $900
notes.choicesExplained: A tests each spouse alone; the joint threshold applies to combined wages. C uses the $200,000 single threshold.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8959 (2025), Additional Medicare Tax, “Threshold Amounts”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Married filing jointly $250,000 Married filing separately $125,000 Single $200,000

notes.front: What are the NIIT threshold amounts?
notes.back: Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse $250,000; married filing separately $125,000; single or head of household $200,000.
notes.explanation: Modified AGI over the threshold is compared with net investment income.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025), Net Investment Income Tax, “Overview”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: • Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse is $250,000. • Married filing separately is $125,000. • Single or head of household is $200,000.

notes.front: What rate is the NIIT, and what is it applied to?
notes.back: 3.8% of the smaller of net investment income or modified AGI over the threshold.
notes.explanation: Both figures are worked out, and only the smaller one is taxed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025), Net Investment Income Tax, “Overview”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: MAGI that's over an applicable threshold amount, and (b) NII, must pay 3.8% of the smaller of (a) or (b) as their NIIT.

notes.front: Ola is single with modified AGI of $230,000, including $20,000 of net investment income. What is her NIIT?
notes.choicesExplained: B applies 3.8% to the $30,000 excess, which is not the smaller figure. C applies 3.8% to all modified AGI.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025), Net Investment Income Tax, “Overview”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: MAGI that's over an applicable threshold amount, and (b) NII, must pay 3.8% of the smaller of (a) or (b) as their NIIT.

notes.front: A couple filing jointly has modified AGI of $270,000 and $40,000 of net investment income. What is their NIIT?
notes.choicesExplained: B applies 3.8% to all $40,000 of investment income instead of the smaller $20,000 excess. C applies 3.8% to $70,000, the excess over the single $200,000 threshold, and skips the smaller-of rule.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025), Net Investment Income Tax, “Overview”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: • Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse is $250,000.

notes.front: How do the NIIT and the Additional Medicare Tax differ in rate and form?
notes.back: NIIT: 3.8%, Form 8960, on investment income. Additional Medicare Tax: 0.9%, Form 8959, on wages and self-employment income.
notes.explanation: They are separate taxes with largely matching thresholds; for a qualifying surviving spouse the NIIT threshold is $250,000 but the Additional Medicare Tax threshold is $200,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8959 (2025), Additional Medicare Tax, “Additional Medicare Tax”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: A 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to your Medicare wages, Railroad Retirement Tax Act (RRTA) compensation, and self-employment income above a threshold amount.

notes.front: When must a church designate a minister’s housing allowance?
notes.back: Officially, as a definite amount, before it makes the payment.
notes.explanation: It can’t set the amount at a later date.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Designation requirement”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The church or organization that employs you must officially designate the payment as a housing allowance before it makes the payment. It must designate a definite amount.

notes.front: What is the most a minister can exclude as a housing allowance?
notes.back: The smallest of: the amount designated, the amount actually used to provide the home, and its fair rental value with furnishings plus utilities.
notes.explanation: Each figure caps the exclusion, and the amount must also not be more than reasonable pay for the services; any excess allowance is included in income.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Exclusion of Rental Allowance”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The amount you exclude can't be more than the fair rental value of the home, including furnishings, plus the cost of utilities.

notes.front: Pastor Ruth’s church paid her salary all year and in December voted to call $18,000 of it a housing allowance. Can she exclude the $18,000?
notes.back: B: no; the designation came after the payments.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No: without prior designation her total salary is income
notes.choicesExplained: A: the church can’t set the amount at a later date.
notes.explanation: Without a definite amount designated in advance, the whole salary is included in income.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Designation requirement”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: If the church or organization doesn't officially designate a definite amount as a housing allowance, you must include your total salary in your income.

notes.front: A minister’s church properly designates $30,000 as a housing allowance and she spends it all on her rented home. Fair rental value with furnishings plus utilities is $24,000. What is the most she may exclude?
notes.choicesExplained: A exceeds the fair-rental-value cap. C is the part she must include.
notes.explanation: Exclusion capped at $24,000; $30,000 − $24,000 = $6,000 stays in income.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Exclusion of Rental Allowance”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The amount you exclude can't be more than the fair rental value of the home, including furnishings, plus the cost of utilities.

notes.front: How are a minister’s earnings from ministerial services treated for social security?
notes.back: As self-employment earnings (ministerial earnings), subject to self-employment tax unless exempt.
notes.explanation: Pub. 517 calls these ministerial earnings.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Table 1”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Ministerial earnings are the self-employment earnings that result from ministerial services

notes.front: By when must a minister file Form 4361 to request exemption from self-employment tax?
notes.back: By the due date (with extensions) of the return for the second year with at least $400 of net self-employment earnings, some ministerial.
notes.explanation: The exemption also requires conscientious or religious opposition to public insurance.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Table 2. The Exemption Quick Reference”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: File by the due date (including extensions) of your income tax return for the second tax year in which you had at least $400 of net earnings from self-employment, any of which came from ministerial services

notes.front: Rev. Adams, ordained in 2023, had $400+ of net ministerial self-employment earnings in 2024 and 2025. By when must he file Form 4361?
notes.back: B: by the due date of his 2025 return, including extensions.
notes.choices:
A) The 2024 return’s due date, with extensions
B) The 2025 return’s due date, with extensions
C) At any time
notes.choicesExplained: A is the first such year, not the second. C is the rule for Form 4029, not Form 4361.
notes.explanation: 2024 is the first year with $400 or more; 2025 is the second.
notes.source: Publication 517 (2025), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers, “Table 2. The Exemption Quick Reference”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: File by the due date (including extensions) of your income tax return for the second tax year in which you had at least $400 of net earnings from self-employment, any of which came from ministerial services

notes.front: Which combat zone pay can an enlisted member exclude from income?
notes.back: Active duty pay earned in any month they served in a combat zone.
notes.explanation: Warrant officers and commissioned warrant officers get the same treatment.
notes.source: Publication 3 (2025), Armed Forces' Tax Guide, “Combat Zone Exclusion”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: you can exclude the following amounts from your income. • Active duty pay earned in any month you served in a combat zone.

notes.front: How is a commissioned officer’s combat zone exclusion limited?
notes.back: To the highest rate of enlisted pay (plus imminent danger/hostile fire pay) for each month of combat zone service.
notes.explanation: Commissioned warrant officers are not subject to this limit.
notes.source: Publication 3 (2025), Armed Forces' Tax Guide, “Commissioned officers”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: The amount of your exclusion is limited to the highest rate of enlisted pay (plus imminent danger/hostile fire pay you received) for each month

notes.front: Sergeant Diaz, enlisted, served in a designated combat zone from 28 to 30 June 2025, then left. How much of her June active duty pay can she exclude?
notes.back: C: all of June’s active duty pay.
notes.choices:
A) None; she served under a month
B) Only the 3 days’ pay
C) All of June’s active duty pay
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: service in any part of the month is enough for an enlisted member.
notes.explanation: The exclusion covers active duty pay for any month she served in a combat zone.
notes.source: Publication 3 (2025), Armed Forces' Tax Guide, “Combat Zone Exclusion”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: you can exclude the following amounts from your income. • Active duty pay earned in any month you served in a combat zone.

notes.front: Who includes income in respect of a decedent in income?
notes.back: The estate if it receives it; a beneficiary who receives it directly; or anyone the estate distributes the right to.
notes.explanation: It is not on the decedent’s final return.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “How To Report”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Income in respect of a decedent must be included in the income of one of the following. • The decedent's estate, if the estate receives it.

notes.front: Where can an individual claim the deduction for estate tax paid on IRD?
notes.back: Only as an itemized deduction, on line 16 of Schedule A (Form 1040).
notes.explanation: Estates claim it on Form 1041 instead.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Estate Tax Deduction”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Individuals can claim this deduction only as an itemized deduction on line 16 of Schedule A (Form 1040).

notes.front: Leo, a cash-basis employee, died in October 2025. His final pay cheque was paid to his estate in November. How is it treated?
notes.back: B: it is income in respect of a decedent, included by the estate that received it.
notes.choices:
A) On Leo’s final return
B) As IRD, included in the estate’s income
C) Not taxable
notes.choicesExplained: A: it wasn’t properly includible on his final return. C: IRD is still income to the recipient.
notes.explanation: Income he would have received but for his death, received by the estate.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Income in Respect of a Decedent”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: All income the decedent would have received had death not occurred that wasn't properly includible on the final return, discussed earlier, is income in respect of a decedent.

notes.front: Which form figures your share of social security and Medicare tax when your employer didn’t withhold it from your wages?
notes.back: Form 8919.
notes.explanation: The result goes on Schedule 2, line 6.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 2, Line 6”, PDF p. 112
notes.evidence: employer who didn't withhold social security and Medicare tax from your wages, use Form 8919 to figure your share of the unreported tax.

notes.front: Which form must you file if you didn’t report all your tips to your employer?
notes.back: Form 4137.
notes.explanation: It is also needed if your Form W-2, box 8, shows allocated tips you must report.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Social security and Medicare tax on tip income”, PDF p. 101
notes.evidence: didn't report all of those tips to your employer, you must file Form 4137.

notes.front: Jana was paid as an employee, but her employer withheld no social security or Medicare tax. How does she pay her share?
notes.back: A: Form 8919, with the tax on Schedule 2, line 6.
notes.choices:
A) Form 8919, carried to Schedule 2
B) Self-employment tax, as if self-employed
C) Nothing is due
notes.choicesExplained: B treats her as self-employed, but she was an employee. C: her share is still owed.
notes.explanation: Form 8919 figures an employee’s share of the unreported tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 2, Line 6”, PDF p. 112
notes.evidence: Include on line 6 the amount from line 13 of Form 8919.
